title: Advanced single-and dual-atom nanomaterials for Hg( ii ) sensing and removal: recognition mechanisms, analytical performance, and practical challenges
content: Developing sensitive, selective, and practically applicable materials for detecting and removing mercury(ii) ions remains crucial for the monitoring and remediation of this toxic environmental contaminant. This review critically examines advances in single-atom and dual-atom materials, nanozymes, metal nanoparticles, carbon dots, functional polymers, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), covalent organic frameworks (COFs), and related porous materials covering literature through 2026, including foundational studies. Representative studies are compared based on Hg2+ recognition mechanism, structure–property relationships, detection limits, selectivity, adsorption capacities, real-sample application and operational stability. Special emphasis is placed on the Hg–S coordination, T–Hg2+–T interactions, metal–Hg interactions, and catalytic, optical and electrochemical signal transduction mechanisms. This review highlights how coordination-engineering, heteroatom configuration, defect sites, and metal–support interactions influence sensing and removal performance. Although several platforms attempt to detect picomolar levels under optimized conditions, matrix effects, limited long term stability, complexity of preparation, and lack of scalability frequently remain major challenges. Furthermore, favorable laboratory detection limits and spike recoveries are insufficient to demonstrate reliability in complex environmental or biological matrices. Biomass-derived materials are potentially cost-effective alternatives, and atomically engineered and porous frameworks enable enhanced recognition and multiple-sensing-removal capabilities. This review offers a mechanism-based comparative perspective and identifies real sample validation, reproducible synthesis, low-cost fabrication, and operational durability as a major priority for developing reliable and salable Hg2+ monitoring and remediation technologies.
